analysis.one_liner: Banned the pesticide daminozide (Alar) from food use and made the maker buy back unsold stock.
analysis.headline: The daminozide ban never left the Senate Agriculture Committee and died without a vote when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The EPA had concluded that the pesticide daminozide, sold as Alar and used mainly on apples, may pose an unreasonable health risk, and had proposed to cancel it — but its own process could take up to 18 months. This bill would have made the ban immediate: it would prohibit any sale or use of daminozide on food, treat its registration as canceled, order a recall and proper disposal paid for by the maker, require the manufacturer to reimburse anyone holding the product at its sale price, and wipe out the legal residue limits for daminozide in food. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially children who eat apples and apple products, would get faster protection from a pesticide the EPA has said may pose an unreasonable health risk. Growers whose sales were collapsing because of consumer fear would also benefit from a swift, definitive removal of the chemical from the food supply.

how_it_helps.text: It bans the distribution, sale, or use of any daminozide pesticide labeled for food use immediately, instead of waiting for the EPA's cancellation process, which the bill notes could take up to 18 months [S2][S3].

It orders the manufacturer to recall existing stocks, pay for proper storage and disposal, and reimburse every person holding the pesticide at the prevailing sale price, so dealers and farmers are not stuck with worthless inventory [S2][S3].

It treats all legal residue limits (tolerances) for daminozide in food as revoked, while letting the Secretary of Health and Human Services set temporary 'action levels' so already-treated food already in commerce can still be sold as residues decline [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The manufacturer of daminozide would bear the cost: an immediate loss of its food-use registration, mandatory recall and disposal expenses, and buyback payments at the sale price for every gallon held by dealers and growers. Growers lose access to the product, though the bill's own findings say they were already losing sales to consumer fear.
analysis.who_pays_short: The chemical's manufacturer and its users

drawbacks.text: The bill short-circuits the EPA's own administrative cancellation process, which the bill acknowledges may take up to 18 months; bypassing that review with a statutory deadline gives the agency less room to complete its scientific record, though the EPA had already determined the use may pose an unreasonable risk [S2][S3].
The mandatory reimbursement at prevailing sale price is an open-ended liability for the registrant, covering every holder of the pesticide, with no cap on total cost [S2][S3].
Growers lose a growth-regulating product they were actively using, and the action-level system means food already treated before the ban could still enter commerce for some time [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case for acting fast was strong — the EPA itself had found an unreasonable risk and its own process was slow — and the bill was deliberately designed to shift the financial burden of the ban onto the manufacturer rather than dealers and farmers. The main costs are the bypass of the EPA's administrative process and the uncapped buyback obligation, both reasonable prices for removing a suspected food hazard faster.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Warner introduced the bill on May 18, 1989, joined by three Democratic and one Republican cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S1][S5].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action of any kind after the referral [S5].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, with the bill still pending in committee, so it never received a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The pesticide's manufacturer and its food-use customers were better off, because no immediate ban with a mandatory buyback ever took effect and any change would come only through the slower EPA process the bill was written to short-cut. Consumers continued to rely on that slower agency route instead of the immediate statutory ban.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The pesticide maker and its customers

for.name: Sen. John Warner
for.role: U.S. Senator from Virginia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban daminozide from food use and referred it to the Agriculture Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 18, 1989; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five sponsors split evenly by party — two Republicans (Warner, Chafee) and three Democrats (Reid, Lieberman, Riegle) — and its death in committee was not a partisan vote because no vote ever occurred [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would immediately cancel the food-use registration, force a company-funded recall and disposal, and require reimbursement of every holder at the sale price. Its gain in continuing sales would come from keeping a chemical the EPA had determined may pose an unreasonable health risk in the food supply.

industries.industry: Apple and other fruit growers using daminozide
industries.note: Growers would lose a growth regulator they used on fruit, but the bill's own findings state that public fear over daminozide was already causing significant economic losses from diminished sales, and an immediate ban was aimed at restoring consumer confidence. On balance the growers' interest in regaining consumer trust ran alongside the public's interest in removing the residue.
